A seventy-year-old looks back and divides his life into periods according to the succession of his masters—that is, according to the regimes he has lived through:
Childhood, 1888–1900: an Eifel-Moselle family Catholicism transplanted into the Sauerland and shaped by rebellion against the state.
Boyhood, 1900–1907: the clericalism of the Catholic boarding school, stripped of its claim to total authority and made relative by a humanist education.
Youth, 1907–1918: a Greater Prussianism of the Wilhelmine kind, stripped of Hegel, together with Neo-Kantianism.
Manhood, 1919–1932: German identity stripped of Prussianism, combined with Weimar-style liberal democracy and strong nationalist reactions, especially anti-Versailles feeling.
Mature years, 1933–1945: unleashed Greater German nationalism in the style of Brother Straubinger, accompanied by an inward retreat.
Later years, 1945–1958: unleashed antifascism, with a charity pension under Article 131.
Good-natured older priests with memories of the Kulturkampf.
Boarding-school directors and patriarchal factory owners.
Wilhelmine officials and officers—basically quite easy-going people.
Genuine pluralism, with a great deal of freedom.
Party bosses, colossal careerists, and lunatics.
Shylocks and persecutors who have been superficially “Nathanized.”
An anxious question from the seventy-year-old:
Will I live to see the de-Nathanization of Germany?

According to the circumstances and the truth of the matter, although he was forced, he nevertheless willed it—whether conditionally or absolutely. Here lies the true source and practical end result of all Vitoria’s beautiful arguments in De Indis, and of his supposed founding of modern international law.
